Graph Mixture of Experts:
Learning on Large-Scale Graphs with Explicit Diversity Modeling

Haotao Wang Affiliation: University of Texas at Austin    Ziyu Jiang Affiliation: Texas A&M University    Yan Han Affiliation: University of Texas at Austin    Zhangyang Wang Affiliation: University of Texas at Austin Correspondence to: atlaswang@utexas.edu
Abstract

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely applied to learning over graph data. Yet, real-world graphs commonly exhibit diverse graph structures and contain heterogeneous nodes and edges. Moreover, to enhance the generalization ability of GNNs, it has become common practice to further increase the diversity of training graph structures by incorporating graph augmentations and/or performing large-scale pre-training on more graphs. Therefore, it becomes essential for a GNN to simultaneously model diverse graph structures. Yet, naively increasing the GNN model capacity will suffer from both higher inference costs and the notorious trainability issue of GNNs. This paper introduces the Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) idea to GNNs, aiming to enhance their ability to accommodate the diversity of training graph structures, without incurring computational overheads. Our new Graph Mixture of Expert (GMoE) model enables each node in the graph to dynamically select its own optimal information aggregation experts. These experts are trained to model different subgroups of graph structures in the training set. Additionally, GMoE includes information aggregation experts with varying aggregation hop sizes, where the experts with larger hop sizes are specialized in capturing information over longer ranges. The effectiveness of GMoE is verified through experimental results on a large variety of graph, node, and link prediction tasks in the OGB benchmark. For instance, it enhances ROC-AUC by 1.81%1.81\% in ogbg-molhiv and by 1.40%1.40\% in ogbg-molbbbp, as compared to the non-MoE baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/Graph-Mixture-of-Experts.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Graph learning has found extensive use in various real-world applications, including recommendation systems (Wu et al., 2022), traffic prediction (Jiang & Luo, 2022), molecular property prediction (Wieder et al., 2020), and sentence structure analysis (Wu et al., 2023). Real-world graph data typically exhibit diverse graph structures and heterogeneous nodes and edges. In graph-based recommendation systems, for instance, a node can represent a product or a customer, while an edge can indicate different interactions such as viewed, liked, or purchased. Similarly, in biochemistry tasks, datasets often comprise molecules with various biochemistry properties and, thus, various graph structures.

Moreover, purposefully increasing the diversity of graph data structures in training sets has become a crucial aspect of GNN training. Techniques like random graph data augmentations (e.g., edge and node dropping) (Han et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022) and large-scale pre-training on diverse graphs (You et al., 2020a; You et al., 2020b; You et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2022) have been widely adopted to augment the diversity of training graph structures. Training on such diverse graph data allows GNNs to extract important features from various graph structures, resulting in more robust and generalizable models. In light of this, we pose the crucial question: Can we create a GNN model architecture that can more effectively leverage and benefit from diverse training samples without any additional computational overhead? 11 1 We aim to avoid introducing computational overhead during the test time, as real-world GNN applications, such as recommendation systems and molecule virtual screening, usually involve processing a vast number of candidate samples, whose inference efficiency is therefore highly desirable (Shen et al., 2021; Hoang et al., 2022; Gentile et al., 2022).

One limitation of many previous GNN architectures is that they are essentially “ homogeneous” across the whole graph, i.e., forcing all nodes to share the same aggregation mechanism, regardless of the differences in their node features or neighborhood information. When training on diverse graph structures, conflicts may arise. For example, some nodes may require information aggregated over longer ranges, while others may demand shorter-range local information.

To enhance the ability of GNN models to leverage and benefit from the structural diversity present in training graphs, we propose a novel architecture called Graph Mixture of Experts (GMoE). Inspired by the recent progress of MoEs in large language models  (Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2022; Roller et al., 2021), GMoE comprises multiple “experts” at each layer, with each expert being an independent aggregation function with its own trainable parameters. During training, the model learns to select the most appropriate aggregation experts for each node, resulting in nodes with similar neighborhood information being routed to the same aggregation experts. In this way, each expert is trained to focus on its own subgroup of training samples that share similar neighborhood information pattern (e.g., shorter or longer range, less or more to aggregate). To further take advantage of the diversity, GMoE employs aggregation experts with different inductive biases. Specifically, each layer of GMoE includes aggregation experts with varying aggregation hop sizes, where experts with larger hop sizes focus on nodes requiring longer-range information and vice versa.

The effectiveness of our method is validated by extensive experiments on ten graph learning datasets in the OGB benchmark. For example, GMoE improves the ROC-AUC by 1.81%1.81\% on ogbg-molhiv, 1.40%1.40\% on ogbg-molbbbp, 0.95%0.95\% on ogbn-proteins, and Hits@20 score by 0.89%0.89\% on ogbl-ddi, as compared to the single-expert baseline. To gain a better understanding of our method, we also carry out more ablation studies and perform analysis.

2 Related Work

2.1 Graph Neural Networks

In recent years, graph neural networks (GNNs) (Kipf & Welling, 2016a; Veličković et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2018) have emerged as a powerful approach for learning graph representations. An iterative neighborhood scheme is followed to capture the structural information within nodes’ neighborhood. Variants of GNNs have been proposed (Kipf & Welling, 2016a; Veličković et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2018), achieving state-of-the-art performance in different graph tasks. Under the framework of message passing mechanism (Gilmer et al., 2017), graph convolutional network (GCN) adopts mean pooling to aggregate the neighborhood information, and updates embeddings layer-by-layer recursively (Kipf & Welling, 2016a); GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017) adopts sampling and aggregation schemes to eliminate the inductive bias in degree; and graph attention network (GAT) utilizes the learnable attention weights to adaptively aggregate; to capture long-range dependencies in disassortative graphs, Geom-GCN devises a geometric aggregation scheme (Pei et al., 2020) to enhance the convolution, benefiting from a continuous space underlying the graph. Graphormer (Ying et al., 2021) proposes a novel graph transformer model that utilizes attention mechanisms to capture the structural information of graphs.

Pre-training of GNNs

Recently, the pre-training of GNN begins to gain popularity. Especially, the unsupervised pre-training methods (You et al., 2020a) are much more popular than their supervised counterpart (Hu et al., 2019) given they are able to utilize the huge data without labels. The unsupervised pre-training methods can be further separated into two categories: contrastive and generative. Contrastive methods perform self-supervised learning by pulling different views of the same graph together while pushing the different views apart (Sun et al., 2019; Velickovic et al., 2019; You et al., 2020a; Qiu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021). In contrast, generative method is devised to reconstruct the input data (Garcia Duran & Niepert, 2017; Kipf & Welling, 2016b; Pan et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019; Salehi & Davulcu, 2019; Hu et al., 2020b; Tang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2017; You et al., 2018a; You et al., 2018b; Hou et al., 2022). We employ the state-of-the-art pre-training method GraphMAE (Hou et al., 2022) to examine if the proposed GMoE can leverage the diversity of huge pre-training dataset.

2.2 Mixture of Experts

The idea of Mixture of Experts (MoE) (Jacobs et al., 1991) can be dated back long  (Jordan & Jacobs, 1994; Chen et al., 1999; Yuksel et al., 2012). Recently, starting from large language models, sparse MoE (Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2022; Roller et al., 2021) only activates a few experts per input, which substantially improves the efficiency and thus enables scaling to gigantic models with trillions of parameters, facilitating the learning process on huge language datasets (Clark et al., 2022; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Following works further improved the stability and efficiency of sparse MoE (Lewis et al., 2021; Zoph et al., 2022). The success of sparse MoE on language sparked its application in other domains such as vision (Riquelme et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020), multi-modal (Mustafa et al., 2022), and multi-task learning (Ma et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022).

Mixture of Experts in GNN

In the graph domain, previous works utilized the knowledge from multiple ranges by merging different GNN with different ranges (Abu-El-Haija et al., 2019; Abu-El-Haija et al., 2020), which can be viewed as MoE with fixed weights. Several pioneer works (Hu et al., 2022a; Zhou et al., 2022) also considered leveraging MoE for addressing the notorious imbalance issue and developing unbiased classification or generalization algorithms. However, none of them utilized the potential benefits of sparsity. In this work, we take a further step to scale graph neural networks with sparse MoE for efficient learning on datasets with diverse graph data. Meanwhile, we also incorporate experts with different ranges. Therefore, the gating function can select the neighbors with desired range adaptively.

Although the experts learned in sparse MoE (Shazeer et al., 2017) are not explicitly trained with different data splits as in traditional dense MoE (Jacobs et al., 1991), there are evidences demonstrating that sparse MoE can divide-and-conquer various semantic concepts for different experts. For instance,  Hu et al. (2022b) manage to learn distinct causal knowledge for different experts. LIMoE (Mustafa et al., 2022) shows that the tokens with different semantic meanings can be assigned to different experts. These facts demonstrate the potential of sparse MoE on handling heterogeneity of graph data.

2.3 Better Model Structures to Embrace Training Sample Diversity

Several previous works studied how to improve deep neural networks’ capability to benefit from diverse training samples while not introducing any inference overhead. Xie et al. (2020) proposed to use two separate batch normalization (BN) layers for randomly and adversarially augmented training samples, motivated by the observation that those two groups of augmented samples are from different distributions. Wang et al. (2021) developed the above idea by introducing an auxiliary instance normalization layer to further reduce the heterogeneity of input features to the BN layers. Recently, Wang et al. (2022) showed that normalizer-free convolutional networks (CNNs) (Brock et al., 2021a; Brock et al., 2021b) have much stronger capability to fit diverse training sets compared with traditional BN-based CNNs. These previous works mainly focus on designing better normalization strategies for CNNs. However, it remains unclear how to generalize this idea to GNNs, where BN is not always a building block. In this paper, we show that our GMoE can address the diversity challenge well on GNNs.

3 Method

In this section, we first provide preliminaries on GNNs in Section 3.1. Then, we present the proposed GMoE in section 3.2. The computation complexity analysis is provided in section 3.3. Lastly, we show how to combine GMoE with graph pre-training techniques in section 3.4.

3.1 Preliminaries: Graph Neural Networks

Taking the traditional Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) proposed in (Kipf & Welling, 2016a) as an example, its propagation rule can be formulated as

hi′=σ⁡(∑j∈Ni1|Ni|​|Nj|​hj​W(i))h_{i}^{\prime}=\sigma\left(\sum_{j\in N_{i}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{|N_{i}||N_{j}|}}h_{j}W^{(i)}\right) (1)

where W(i)∈ℝs×sW^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times s} is a trainable weight and σ\sigma is an element-wise non-linear activation function. hj∈ℝb×sh_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times s} denotes the input feature of jj th node while hi′∈ℝb×sh_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times s} is its output feature in ii th node. bb and ss are batch size and hidden feature size, respectively. NiN_{i} denotes the collection of neighbors for ii th node including self-connection. The output feature is then normalized with 1|Ni|​|Nj|\frac{1}{\sqrt{|N_{i}||N_{j}|}}. Given the traditional GCN only aggregates the information from adjacent neighbors, it is a hop-1 graph convolutional layer.

Mixhop (Abu-El-Haija et al., 2019) further proposed hop-2 Graph Convolutional Networks, which can be formulated as

hi′=σ⁡(∑j∈Ni21|Ni|​|Nj|​hj​W(i))h_{i}^{\prime}=\sigma\left(\sum_{j\in N^{2}_{i}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{|N_{i}||N_{j}|}}h_{j}W^{(i)}\right) (2)

where Ni2N^{2}_{i} denotes nodes with a minimum distance of 2 to the ii th node. it would consider a long-range relationship with a distance of 2. Combining hop-1 and hop-2 convolutional layers can be proved to be more expressive than the traditional GCN. For instance, it can model more operations like Delta Operators (Abu-El-Haija et al., 2019).

3.2 Graph Mixture of Experts

The general framework of GMoE can be seen in Figure 1. The GMoE layer comprises multiple experts, each utilizing either the hop-1 or hop-2 aggregation function. To determine which experts to use for a given node, a gating function is employed. This allows for similar nodes to be assigned to the same experts when learning with diverse graph structures, thereby enabling each expert to specialize in a particular structure type. By doing so, the model can more effectively capture diverse graph structures present within the training set. The GMoE layer’s adaptive selection between the hop-1 and hop-2 experts enables the model to dynamically capture short-range or long-range information aggregation for each node.

Formally, the proposed GMoE layer can be defined as

hi′=σ(∑o=1m∑j∈NiG​(hi)o​Eo​(hj,ei​j,W)+CLOSEOPEN∑o=mn∑j∈Ni2G​(hi)o​Eo​(hj,ei​j,W))\begin{split}h^{\prime}_{i}=\sigma&\left(\sum_{o=1}^{m}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}G(h_{i})_{o}E_{o}\left(h_{j},e_{ij},W\right)+\right.\\ &\left.\sum_{o=m}^{n}\sum_{j\in N^{2}_{i}}G(h_{i})_{o}E_{o}\left(h_{j},e_{ij},W\right)\right)\end{split} (3)

where mm and nn denote the hop-1 and total experts number, respectively. Hench the number of hop-2 experts is n−mn-m. EoE_{o} and ei​je_{ij} denote the message function and edge feature between ii th and jj th nodes, respectively. It can represent multiple kinds of message-passing functions like the one employed for the traditional GCN (Li et al., 2020) or GIN (Xu et al., 2018). GG is the gating function that generates multiple decision scores with the input of hih_{i} while G​(hi)oG(h_{i})_{o} denotes the oo th item in the output vector of GG. We employ the noisy top-k gating design for GG following (Shazeer et al., 2017), which can be formalized with

G⁡(hi)=Softmax⁡(TopK⁡(Q⁡(hi),k))G(h_{i})=\operatorname{Softmax}(\operatorname{TopK}(Q(h_{i}),k)) (4)
Q⁡(hi)=hi​Wg+ϵ⋅Softplus⁡(hi​Wn)Q(h_{i})=h_{i}W_{g}+\epsilon\cdot\operatorname{Softplus}(h_{i}W_{n}) (5)

where kk denotes the number of selected experts. ϵ∈𝒩⁡(0,1)\epsilon\in\mathcal{N}\left(0,1\right) denotes standard Gaussian noise. Wg∈ℝs×nW_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times n} and Wn∈ℝs×nW_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times n} are learnable weights that control clean and noisy scores, respectively. TopK\operatorname{TopK} function is defined as

 TopK ​(v,k)o={vo if ​vo​ is in the top ​k​ elements of ​v−∞ otherwise. \text{ TopK }(v,k)_{o}=\begin{cases}v_{o}&\text{ if }v_{o}\text{ is in the top }k\text{ elements of }v\\ -\infty&\text{ otherwise. }\end{cases} (6)

for ensuring that, after passing softmax, only kk experts are with a positive score while others are 0.

The proposed GMoE layer can be applied to multiple kinds of GNN like GIN (Xu et al., 2018) or GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2016a). In practice, we replace every layer of the origin GNN with its corresponding GMoE layer. For simplicity, we name the resultant network GMoE-GCN or GMoE-GIN (for GCN and GIN, respectively).

However, when training this model with only expectation-maximization loss, it can easily collapse to a trivial solution that only employs the same group of experts given the self-reinforcing property of this imbalance: the selected experts can grow much faster than others and thusly can be picked more frequently. We further employ two losses for preventing the collapsing following (Shazeer et al., 2017). The first one is importance loss, which is defined as

Importance⁡(H)=∑hi∈H,g∈G⁡(hi)g\operatorname{Importance}(H)=\sum_{h_{i}\in H,g\in G(h_{i})}g (7)
Limportance​(H)=C​V​(Importance⁡(H))2L_{\operatorname{importance}}(H)=CV(\operatorname{Importance}(H))^{2} (8)

where the importance score Importance⁡(H)\operatorname{Importance}(H) is defined as the sum of each node’s gate value gg across the whole batch. C​VCV represents the coefficient of variation function. The importance loss Limportance​(H)L_{\operatorname{importance}}(H) is defined as the coefficient of variation of the importance score, enforcing all experts to have the same importance score.

While the importance score constrains the equal score of the experts, the load for different experts may still differ. For example, one expert can be assigned with several large scores while another one was selected by more nodes with a small score, which can lead to memory or efficiency problems on distributed hardware. Another load-balanced loss is introduced to solve this problem, it encourages each expert to be selected with a similar probability. Specifically, G⁡(hi)≠0G(h_{i})\neq 0 if and only if Q​(hi)oQ(h_{i})_{o} is bigger than k t​hth biggest element of Q⁡(hi)Q(h_{i}) excluding itself. Hence, the probability of G⁡(hi)≠0G(h_{i})\neq 0 can be expressed as

P⁡(hi,o)=P​r​(Q​(hi)o>kth​_​ex⁡(Q⁡(hi),k,o))\begin{split}P(h_{i},o)=Pr(Q(h_{i})_{o}>\operatorname{kth\_ex}(Q(h_{i}),k,o))\end{split} (9)

where k​t​h​_​e​x​(Q⁡(hi),k,o)kth\_ex(Q(h_{i}),k,o) denotes the k t​hth biggest element excluding itself. P⁡(hi,o)P(h_{i},o) can be simplified as

P⁡(hiCLOSE,o)=Φ⁡(hi​Wg−kth​_​ex⁡(Q⁡(hi),k,o)Softplus⁡(hi​Wn))\begin{split}P(h_{i}&,o)=\\ &\Phi\left(\frac{h_{i}W_{g}-\operatorname{kth\_ex}(Q(h_{i}),k,o)}{\operatorname{Softplus}(h_{i}W_{n})}\right)\end{split} (10)

where Φ\Phi is the CDF of standard normal distribution. The load is then defined as the batch-wise sum of the probability score as

Load⁡(H)o=∑hi∈H,p∈P⁡(hi,o)p\operatorname{Load}(H)_{o}=\sum_{h_{i}\in H,p\in P(h_{i},o)}p (11)

where pp is the node-wise probability in the batch. The load loss is then defined as the square of the coefficient of the variation as

Lload​(H)=C​V​(Load⁡(H))2L_{\operatorname{load}}(H)=CV(\operatorname{Load}(H))^{2} (12)

To conclude, in the final loss term, we employ both task-specific loss and two load-balance losses. Formally, the final optimization target is

L=LE​M+λ⁡(Lload​(H)+Limportance​(H))L=L_{EM}+\lambda(L_{\operatorname{load}}(H)+L_{\operatorname{importance}}(H)) (13)

where LE​ML_{EM} denotes the task-specific expectation maximizing loss. λ\lambda is a hand-tuned scaling factor shared by two load-balance losses.

3.3 Efficiency Analysis

In this section, we show that GMoE-GNN brings negligible overhead on computational cost compared with its traditional GNN counterpart. We measure computational cost using the number of floating point operations (FLOPs).

The computation cost of a GMoE layer can be defined as

CG​M​o​E=∑hi∈Hℱ[∑o=1mG(hi)o∑j∈NiEo(hj,ei​j,W)+∑o=mnG(hi)o∑j∈Ni2Eo(hj,ei​j,W)]\begin{split}C_{GMoE}=\sum_{h_{i}\in H}\mathcal{F}&\left[\sum_{o=1}^{m}G(h_{i})_{o}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}E_{o}\left(h_{j},e_{ij},W\right)+\right.\\ &\left.\sum_{o=m}^{n}G(h_{i})_{o}\sum_{j\in N^{2}_{i}}E_{o}\left(h_{j},e_{ij},W\right)\right]\end{split} (14)

where ℱ\mathcal{F} maps functions to its flops number. CG​M​o​EC_{GMoE} denotes the computation cost of the whole layer in GMoE-GCN. Given there exists an efficient algorithm that can solve hop-1 and hop-2 functions with matching computational complexity (Abu-El-Haija et al., 2019), we can further simplify CG​M​o​EC_{GMoE} as

CG​M​o​E=∑hi∈H∑j∈NiC​∑o=1n𝟏​(G​(hi)o)C_{GMoE}=\sum_{h_{i}\in H}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}C\sum_{o=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}(G(h_{i})_{o}) (15)
C=ℱ⁡[Eo​(hj,ei​j,W)]C=\mathcal{F}\left[E_{o}\left(h_{j},e_{ij},W\right)\right] (16)
𝟏​(G​(hi)o)={0 if ​G​(hi)o=01 otherwise. \mathbf{1}(G(h_{i})_{o})=\begin{cases}0&\text{ if }G(h_{i})_{o}=0\\ 1&\text{ otherwise. }\end{cases} (17)

Given ∑o=1n𝟏​(G​(hi)o)=k\sum_{o=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}(G(h_{i})_{o})=k, CG​M​o​EC_{GMoE} can be further simplified to

CG​M​o​E=k​∑hi∈H∑j∈NiC.C_{GMoE}=k\sum_{h_{i}\in H}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}C. (18)

Here, CC is the computation cost of a single message passing in GMoE-GCN. We further define the computation cost of a single message passing in traditional GCN as C0C_{0}, and the total computational cost in the whole layer as CG​C​NC_{GCN}. By setting C=C0kC=\frac{C_{0}}{k} in GMoE-GCN, we have CG​M​o​E=∑hi∈H∑j∈NiC0=CG​C​NC_{GMoE}=\sum_{h_{i}\in H}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}C_{0}=C_{GCN}.

In traditional GMoE-GCN or GMoE-GIN, the adjustment of CC can be easily realized by controlling the hidden feature dimension size ss. For instance, GMoE-GCN and GMoE-GIN with hidden dimension size of s=s0ks=\frac{s_{0}}{\sqrt{k}} can have similar FLOPs with its corresponding GCN and GIN with dimension size of s0s_{0}.

The computation cost of gating functions in GMoE is negligible compared to the cost of selected experts, since both Wg∈ℝn×sW_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times s} and Wn∈ℝn×sW_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times s} is in a much smaller dimension than W(i)∈ℝs×sW^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times s} given n≪sn\ll s.

In conclusion, by reducing the dimension of hidden features by k\sqrt{k} times in GMoE, GMoE-GCN/GIN can achieve similar computational cost with traditional GCN/GIN, with negligible overhead brought by the gating functions.

3.4 Pre-training

We employ GraphMAE proposed by Hou et al., 2022 as the self-supervised pre-training technique. It is a generative pre-training method that reconstructs input from the corrupted input, which can be defined as

ℒ⁡(H,M)=D⁡(d⁡(f⁡(M⋅H)),H)\mathcal{L}\left(H,M\right)=D\left(d\left(f\left(M\cdot H\right)\right),H\right) (19)

where ff and dd denote the encoder and the decoder networks respectively. MM represents the mask for adding noise to the graph HH. ff and dd collaborative conduct the reconstruction task. And the reconstruction quality is measured by the distance metric DD.

4 Results

In this section, we first describe the detailed experimental settings in Section 4.1. We then show our main results on graph learning in Section 4.2. Lastly, ablation studies and analysis are provided in Section 4.3.

4.1 Experimental Settings

Datasets and Evaluation Metrics

We conduct experiments on ten graph datasets in the OGB benchmark (Hu et al., 2020a), including graph-level (i.e., ogbg-bbbp, ogbg-hiv, ogbg-moltoxcast, ogbg-moltox21, ogbg-molesol, and ogbg-freesolv), node-level (i.e., ogbn-protein, ogbn-arxiv), and link-level prediction (i.e., ogbl-ddi, ogbl-ppa) tasks. Following Hu et al. (2020a), we use ROC-AUC (i.e., area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) as the evaluation metric on ogbg-bbbp, ogbg-hiv, ogbg-moltoxcast, ogbg-moltox21, and ogbn-protein; RMSE (i.e., root mean squared error) on ogbg-molesol, and ogbg-freesolv; classification accuracy (Acc) on ogbn-arxiv; Hits@100 score on ogbl-ppa; Hits@20 score on ogbl-ddi.

Model Architectures and Implementation Details for Training

We use the GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2016a) and GIN (Xu et al., 2018) provided by OGB benchmark (Hu et al., 2020a) as the baseline models. All model settings (e.g., number of layers, hidden feature dimensions, etc.) and training hyper-parameters (e.g., learning rates, training epochs, batch size, etc.) are identical as those in Hu et al. (2020a). We show the performance gains brought by their GMoE counterparts: GMoE-GCN and GMoE-GIN. For GMoE models, as described in Section 3, we select kk experts out of a total of nn experts for each node, where mm out of nn experts are hop-1 aggregation functions and the rest n−mn-m are hop-2 aggregation functions. All three hyper-parameters n,m,kn,m,k, together with the loss trade-off weight λ\lambda in Eq. (13), are tuned by grid searching: n∈{4,8}n\in\{4,8\}, m∈{0,n/2,n}m\in\{0,n/2,n\}, k∈{1,2,4}k\in\{1,2,4\}, and λ∈{0.1,1}\lambda\in\{0.1,1\}. The hidden feature dimension would be adjusted with kk (Section 3.3) to ensure the same flops for all comparisons. The hyper-parameter values achieving the best performance on validation sets are selected to report results on test sets, following the routine in Hu et al. (2020a). All other training hyper-parameters on GMoE (e.g., batch size, learning rate, training epochs) are kept the same as those used on the single-expert baselines. All experiments are run for ten times with different random seeds, and we report the mean and deviation of the results following Hu et al. (2020a).

Pre-training Settings

Following the transfer learning setting of (Hu et al., 2019; You et al., 2020a; You et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2022), we pre-train the models on a subset of the ZINC15 dataset (Sterling & Irwin, 2015) containing 2 million unlabeled molecule graphs. For training hyperparameters, we employ a batch size of 1024 to accelerate the training on the large pre-train dataset for both baselines and the proposed method. We follow (Hou et al., 2022) employing GIN (Xu et al., 2018) as the backbone, 0.001 as the learning rate, adam as the optimizer, 0 as the weight decay, 100 as the training epochs number, and 0.25 as the masking ratio.

4.2 Main Results

We first compare our GMoE-GCN with the baseline single-expert GCN on six graph property prediction datasets under the supervised learning setting, where all models are trained from scratch using only the labeled samples in the training set. The results are shown in Table 2. GMoE-GCN achieves general performance gains over all six datasets. For example, it improves ROC-AUC by 1.41%1.41\% and 1.81%1.81\% on molbbp and molhiv datasets, respectively.

Large-scale pretraining on auxiliary unlabeled data has been successfully applied on GNNs to improve the generalization ability by introducing more diverse graph structures during training (You et al., 2020a; You et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2022). In this paragraph, we show that GMoE also achieves consistent performance improvement when combined with large-scale pre-training method. Specifically, we follow (Hou et al., 2022) to use GIN (Xu et al., 2018) as the baseline model and compare it with GMoE-GIN. As shown in Table 3, compared to GIN, the proposed GMoE-GIN achieves performance improvement on 3 out of 4 datasets while improving the average performance by 0.54%0.54\% without pre-training, demonstrating that the proposed GMoE can yield performance improvement on different model types. By further combining with the pre-training method, GMoE-GIN also outperforms the GIN baseline with an even slightly higher improvement margin of 0.6%0.6\%.

We further show GMoE can also benefit node and link prediction on graph data. Specifically, we conduct experiments on ogbn-protein and ogbn-arxiv for node prediction, and ogbl-ddi and ogbl-ppa. The former is a node prediction task to predict the functions of proteins in a protein association graph. The latter is a link prediction task to predict drug-drug interactions. The results are shown in Table 4 and Table 5. GMoE-GCN outperforms the single expert GCN by 0.95%0.95\% ROC-AUC and 0.89%0.89\% Hits@20 on ogbn-protein and ogbl-ddi datasets, respectively.

4.3 Ablation Study and Analysis

In this section, we conduct ablation experiments on the hyper-parameters n,m,kn,m,k in GMoE, and list several interesting observations below.

Observation 1: Larger graphs prefer larger hop sizes

We conduct the ablation study on the two most representative molecule datasets: ogbg-molhiv and ogbg-molfreesolv, which have the largest and smallest average graph sizes among all molecular datasets in the OGB benchmark, respectively. As shown in the third column of Table 6, the molecular graphs in ogbg-molhiv are around three times larger than those in ogbg-molfreesolv dataset in average. On ogbg-molfreesolve, if all experts are hop-2 aggregation functions (i.e., when m=0m=0), the performance is considerably worse compared with using all hop-1 experts (i.e., when m=nm=n). In contrast, on ogbg-molhiv, where the graphs are much larger, using all hop-2 experts (i.e., when m=0m=0) achieves better performance than using all hop-1 experts (i.e., when m=nm=n). This indicates that larger graphs prefer aggregation experts with larger hop sizes. This observation intuitively makes sense, since larger molecular graphs may require more long-range aggregation information compared with smaller molecular graphs.

Observation 2: Sparsity in expert selection is necessary for performance gains

As shown in Table 6, the best performance on both datasets are achieved by sparse MoEs (i.e., when k≠nk\neq n) instead of dense MoEs (i.e., when k=nk=n). This indicates that, compared to dense MoE, the bigger capacity of sparse MoE design can facilitate the understanding on graph dataset, which has a diverse set of training samples.

Observation 3: GMoE achieves performance gains, though taking more epochs to converge

We compare the convergence curve of GMoE-GCN and single expert GCN in Figure 2. Specifically, we plot the validation and test ROC-AUC at different epochs when training on protein dataset. As we can see, the performance of GMoE-GCN plateaus later than that of GCN, but GMoE-GCN finally achieves a considerable performance gain after enough training epochs. We provide our explanation for this phenomenon below. At the early stage of training, each expert in GMoE has been updated for kk times fewer iterations than the single expert GNN. This makes all experts in GMoE weak and thus GMoE performs worse than GCN at this early stage. However, after GMoE has been trained for enough epochs, all experts have been updated for enough iterations, and they have learned to fit their own subgroups of data well. As a result, the performance of GMoE surpasses that of single expert GCN.

Observation 4: Load-balance loss is necessary

We further study the scaling factor for the loading balance loss λ\lambda. As illustrated in Table 7, employing λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 can yield substantially higher performance than λ=0\lambda=0 by surpassing 2.58%2.58\% in terms of ROC-AUC. This indicates the necessity of employing load-balance losses. In contrast, the value of λ\lambda is not very sensitive, picking λ=1\lambda=1 would yield a similar performance of 75.27%75.27\%.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we propose the Graph Mixture of Experts (GMoE) model architecture. GMoE increases the effective capacity of GNN with neglectable computational overhead. Specifically, GMoE would adaptively select a subset of desired experts from a large group of experts for each node according to the context. The experts with multiple hop sizes enable nodes to adaptively choose their hop ranges. Extensive experiments on different datasets and model structures demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, in particular showing GMoE to be compatible and promising for large-scale pre-training.
